prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]

Do not keep the Alzheimer's dementia label and forgo the iNPH work-up when a magnetic gait, urinary urgency and ventriculomegaly with DESH are present, whatever the predominance of the cognitive symptoms
Do not read the cognitive profile as typical amnestic Alzheimer's disease: executive and processing-speed impairment dominate and recall improves with cues
Do not treat the family history of cognitive decline as evidence that this patient has Alzheimer's disease
Do not perform the large-volume lumbar tap before brain MRI has excluded a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 32% in TUG at 24 hours, the DESH MRI (Evans index 0.36, callosal angle 74 degrees) and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]

Revisit the prior diagnosis of early Alzheimer's dementia with the patient and her daughter: the cognitive profile, gait and urinary features, MRI and tap response point to iNPH, and cognition should be reassessed after shunting
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery, given two near-falls and osteoporosis

avoided_actions.rationale: She has no episodes suggesting seizures or fluctuation, so an EEG cannot separate iNPH from Alzheimer's disease.
Her near-falls are trips on carpet without syncope or palpitations, so an ECG does not inform the work-up.
There is no syncope, murmur or embolic event, so echocardiography has no role in this work-up.
An MRI is available and measures the callosal angle, temporal horns, hippocampi and aqueduct better than CT.
The near-falls are not syncopal, so rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role here.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test; the Alzheimer question can be answered on the tap specimen.
A 14-month afebrile decline with a normal CSF cell count gives no indication for prion, inflammatory or infectious assays.

differential.key_features: The prior label rested on cognitive symptoms and family history alone; the dysexecutive profile with cue-responsive recall, MTA 1 hippocampi, DESH and a 32% tap response argue against it as the cause, and CSF amyloid and tau, if measured, are normal.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Fazekas 2 periventricular change and a dysexecutive profile overlap, but ventriculomegaly with DESH and the tap response point to iNPH; a vascular contribution remains possible.
No visual hallucinations, fluctuations, REM sleep behaviour disorder or parkinsonism.
Executive slowing without disinhibition, apathy or loss of empathy, and no frontal or anterior temporal atrophy on MRI.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventricles are enlarged out of proportion to mild cortical volume loss, with tight high-convexity sulci and an acute callosal angle of 74 degrees, and the gait improves after CSF removal.

key_clinical_evidence: Cognitive-predominant iNPH: executive slowing dominates the complaint, while the gait disturbance (short steps, reduced foot clearance, start hesitation) is subtle and must be examined for even when it is not the chief complaint.

The cognitive profile of iNPH is frontal-subcortical: processing speed and executive function are impaired, and free recall is reduced with benefit from cues and preserved recognition, unlike the storage deficit of amnestic Alzheimer's disease.
Family history and an outside Alzheimer's label anchor the case; the full syndrome (gait, cognition, urinary urgency) has to be sought in every patient with ventriculomegaly.

Evans index 0.36 with DESH and a callosal angle of 74 degrees are supportive imaging; with normal-pressure CSF and an objective tap response (TUG 32% faster at 24 hours) they make iNPH probable [Nakajima_2021].

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The prior Alzheimer's label was given without imaging or gait assessment; the magnetic gait, urinary urgency, ventriculomegaly with DESH and the tap response point to iNPH.
red_herrings.data_point: Prior diagnosis of probable early Alzheimer's dementia by geriatric psychiatry two months before admission, based on cognitive symptoms, a bedside screen and family history
red_herrings.intended_effect: All cognitive and motor symptoms are attributed to Alzheimer's disease progression; the ventriculomegaly, DESH, and subtle magnetic gait are ignored or attributed to cerebral atrophy, foreclosing NPH evaluation

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A family history of late-life cognitive decline is a risk factor, not a diagnosis; the magnetic gait, DESH and the objective tap response are more specific evidence for the current syndrome.
red_herrings.data_point: Mother with dementia diagnosed in her late 70s (type unclear) and a sister with mild cognitive impairment
red_herrings.intended_effect: Family history of dementia raises the prior for Alzheimer's disease and reinforces premature closure, leading away from a treatable hydrocephalus syndrome

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]
The timed gait is repeated after the tap, at 2 to 24 hours, so that its change from the baseline measures the response to CSF removal [Nakajima_2021]

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive cognitive slowing and memory difficulties over 14 months, with subtle walking changes noticed by family over the past 6 months

family_history: Mother had dementia, diagnosed in her late 70s (type unclear)

patient.history_present_illness: A 76-year-old retired accountant was admitted for inpatient evaluation of progressive cognitive decline. Over the past 14 months, she has developed worsening 'brain fog,' slowed thinking, difficulty managing her household finances, and increasing trouble following complex conversations. Her daughter, a nurse, noted that her mother had become 'mentally slower' and less able to multitask; she previously balanced family accounts and organized community events independently but now requires help with both. The cognitive decline prompted her primary care physician to refer her to a geriatric psychiatrist, who diagnosed probable early Alzheimer's dementia two months ago based on her prominent cognitive symptoms, a low score on a bedside cognitive screen and a family history of cognitive decline (mother with dementia, sister with mild cognitive impairment). No neuroimaging was obtained at that time. The family accepted this diagnosis and began researching memory care facilities. However, over the past 6 months her daughter has noticed a subtle change in her mother's walking: she now shuffles with small steps and seems to hesitate before stepping off curbs, and her feet appear to 'catch' on the carpet. There have been two near-falls. Additionally, she has developed urinary urgency with two episodes of incontinence over the past 4 months, which she attributes to 'being slow to the bathroom.' Her daughter, concerned that the walking change did not fit the diagnosis, brought her to the emergency department requesting a second opinion on the Alzheimer's diagnosis. The patient herself is concerned about the cognitive changes and eager for evaluation; she denies tremor, sudden falls, visual hallucinations, or asymmetric limb symptoms.
